extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism/media, practicing journalists, and readers interested in the principles of news and public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria and principles for what constitutes news, how newspapers select and present it, and economic/social influences on reporting. Useful for evaluating or producing newspaper journalism and understanding structural constraints on coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metropolitan dailies as primary general news gatherers
rubrics_metrics.description: A relatively small number of city dailies (about 175 in U.S. cities over 100,000) constitute the press for 'general news' and act as the local reporters for newspapers of other cities via press associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These key metropolitan papers collect and distribute reports of great events; national and rural papers take much of their general news from a few metropolitan dailies and press associations. Evaluate reliance on these centers when judging comprehensiveness and sources of a paper's general news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic support determined by advertiser-targeted urban buyers
rubrics_metrics.description: The economic basis for general news gathering comes from advertisers who target the prosperous sections of cities; these buying publics are the primary source of revenue that sustains general-news operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content choices are shaped by the demographic and purchasing power of the advertiser-targeted audience. When assessing editorial choices, consider how advertiser interests and the composition of the paying audience influence what is covered and how.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader loyalty as basis of editorial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper with a devoted, large readership has more independence from advertisers; 'more readers, more independence of the influence of advertisers; fewer readers and more dependence on the advertiser.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loyal circulation can counterbalance advertiser pressure. A paper betraying readers for advertisers likely either shares advertisers' views or fears losing reader support. Evaluate independence by measuring reader commitment and patterns of advertiser influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers' social ties shape editorial perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers are typically members of the urban communities they serve and 'see the world through the lenses of their associates and friends', which influences editorial policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how proprietors' social networks and class/location shape coverage priorities and perspectives, rather than attributing all bias solely to abstract ownership interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper as the 'printed diary of the home town' (personal relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers secure readers by chronicling local, personally relevant events—weddings, funerals, local achievements—because individuals are most interested in items that concern themselves and their neighbors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage that cites local, personally relevant facts builds loyalty. When evaluating reach or audience engagement, consider how much the paper functions as a local diary versus a source of broader public affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readers judge newspapers by handling of issues they feel involved in
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual readers tend to evaluate a newspaper chiefly by how it treats the parts of the news in which they feel personally involved; if a paper's account of their business, church, or party 'checks up' with their own view, they trust it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perceived accuracy and sympathetic framing of locally salient subjects are major determinants of reader trust and subscription behavior; assess local-topic accuracy separately from general-news accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited legal accountability of the general reader
rubrics_metrics.description: General readers have no standing in law for misleading general news; only an aggrieved party can sue for slander or libel and must prove material injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the law treats general news as not of common concern (except immoral/seditious matter), external legal pressures do not enforce accuracy for general reporting; consider alternative accountability mechanisms (internal standards, tribunals, press criticism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes and preconceptions shape acceptance of news
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers are likely to accept news that conforms to their stereotypes and preconceptions; when news aligns with these frames, the canonical test of truth is often suspended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage that fits popular stereotypes meets less skepticism; examine how stereotyping may allow inaccurate or uncritical reporting to persist and how that affects public opinion formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversification into non-political features to hold circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Because political or big-news interest is intermittent, newspapers include features—society pages, sports, comics, advice, cookery, pictures—to sustain steady readership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between editorial choices driven by public-service motives and those driven by the need to retain readers; evaluate the extent to which content mix is chosen to maximize circulation rather than to inform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low pay and status of straight reporting weakens professionalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Straight reporting is the most poorly paid and least regarded branch of newspaper work; able people treat it as temporary, which undermines corporate traditions, standards of admission, and self-regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging reporting quality, consider structural labor factors—pay, career prospects, turnover—that reduce incentives for professionalism, craft pride, and internal enforcement of standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological bias is not explained solely by ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Bias and faults are found across capitalist and anti-capitalist papers alike; attributing all faults to 'Big Business' ignores similar failures in oppositional presses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims about systemic causes of press failure critically; look for evidence that purported causes uniquely explain observed faults before attributing bias to ownership alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: News requires an overt, definable act or manifestation to be reportable
rubrics_metrics.description: Before events become news they usually must take an overt form—bankruptcy filings, arrests, votes, speeches, meetings—that makes them objectifiable and reportable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess newsworthiness by whether an event has a clear, reportable manifestation. Absence of such a manifestation often keeps matters out of daily reportage until an overt signal appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of a record-keeping system increases certainty and coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Topics with robust recording machinery (stock tickers, election returns, vital records, customs logs) produce precise, dependable news; where an apparatus exists, the service can report with accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims of accuracy, consider if there is an institutional record that supports reportage; stronger records usually yield more reliable, immediate news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of records makes certain topics debatable or neglected
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects like states of mind, motives, internal trade, working conditions, or public feeling are poorly recorded and thus become debatable, speculative, or neglected in routine news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether lack of objective metrics or records explains underreporting or contested accounts; investigative work or organized claims are often needed to convert these matters into reportable news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press agents filter and shape information; they act as censors/propagandists
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicity men present reporters with a formulated picture of events designed to show the employer's interests; they act as gatekeepers, 'responsible only to his employers' conception of their interests.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate source provenance and consider how press-agent framing may omit or bias facts; recognize institutionalized publicity as a routine intermediary in modern news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity stunts manufacture news value
rubrics_metrics.description: To secure free publicity a press agent must 'start something'—arrange stunts or create events that tie a client to an already newsworthy type of incident (obstruct traffic, provoke police reaction, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to manufactured events and stunts as sources of coverage; distinguish between spontaneous news and publicity-engineered incidents when assessing authenticity and public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative reporting requires substantial resources and is uncommon in dailies
rubrics_metrics.description: In-depth investigations (Pittsburgh Surveys, Interchurch Steel Reports) demand time, money, specialized talent, and space—resources most daily newspapers lack for continual application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that complex, truth-seeking journalism will be episodic and resource-constrained in routine dailies; evaluate claims of comprehensiveness against resource requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine reporting stylizes raw material rather than mirroring social conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Daily journalism typically reports stylized, obtrusive aspects of events (the 'sprout breaking the surface'), not the underlying, gradual social processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether reporting reflects reality, recognize that routine coverage highlights salient, manifest stages rather than the full causal complexity; treat such reports as snapshots, not complete analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporters rely on stereotyped 'shapes' of events and overt phases, simplifying complex issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Because events often must assume a definable shape to be news, reporting reduces complex struggles (e.g., strikes) to overt episodes, catchwords, and their immediate effects on readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether coverage reduces nuanced conflicts to familiar tropes and whether central issues are omitted from headlines and leads. Deeper context often requires deliberate investigatory reporting beyond routine dispatches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skilled journalists anticipate and recognize early signs of news
rubrics_metrics.description: Good reporters detect news before it fully 'assumes a shape'—they notice indicators (dangerous building lists, inquiries about climates) and can forecast events that will become news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate individual reporter skill in sourcing and anticipation; newsrooms that prize such skill can surface important stories earlier than competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press service standardization homogenizes big-news coverage; papers differentiate via other content
rubrics_metrics.description: Wire services and press associations standardize main events, so competition in big news is limited; newspapers therefore differentiate themselves with other features (society pages, specialized columns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing outlets, account for the homogenizing influence of wire services on 'big news' and examine what unique features a paper offers to attract readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader's personal experience colors the interpretation and interest of news
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers inject their own experiences into abstract reports (e.g., interpreting a strike as inconvenience or threat), making local/interested perspectives dominate how news is received and understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess public reaction and perceived significance of stories by considering typical readers' experiences; editorial choices often cater to these reactions to enlist interest.
